p.x:
Last month, I had my first job interview. The position was a receptionist at a small hotel in Chiang Mai. I prepared for days. I read about the hotel online, updated my CV, and practised answering questions with my sister. I also bought new clothes: a white shirt and black trousers.
On the day of the interview, I was ready thirty minutes early. The manager was very friendly and polite. She asked me about my studies and why I wanted to work in a hotel. I tried to speak slowly and listen carefully to every question. She also asked me to write a short email in English.
Two days later, the hotel called me. "We'd like to offer you the job," the manager said. I accepted immediately! Now I'm an employee at the hotel, and my employer is happy with my work. My advice? Prepare well, and be yourself.

Most interviews include a few difficult questions. Preparing your answers can make a big difference.
"What are your strengths and weaknesses?" This is one of the most common questions. For strengths, give real examples: if you say you have leadership skills, describe a time you led a group project. For weaknesses, be honest but positive. Explain what you are doing to improve.
"Tell me about a time you worked in a team." Employers value teamwork, so prepare a short story, perhaps from an internship or a university club. Show that you are reliable and that you listened to others.
"Why should we choose you rather than another applicant?" Here, you need to be enthusiastic without sounding arrogant. Mention what makes you different and how you can help the company.
Remember that the interviewer may also contact your reference, so never exaggerate your experience. And be careful what you say about your last job: an applicant who complains about being fired from a previous company rarely makes a good impression.

For many large companies, recruitment is a long and careful process. A single advertisement can attract thousands of applications, so the first step is often automatic: software scans CVs for key words and credentials such as degrees, languages or certificates. Only a small percentage of applicants make the shortlist.
At the interview stage, employers look beyond qualifications. They want people who are competent, of course, but also articulate: able to explain ideas clearly to colleagues and clients. Many companies now value "soft skills" as highly as technical ones. Can the candidate collaborate with people from different backgrounds? Do they show initiative, or do they wait for instructions?
Interviewers also try to judge personality. A proactive, motivated candidate who asks thoughtful questions about the company is likely to impress. Being ambitious is generally seen as positive, as long as the candidate seems willing to work hard rather than simply wanting a quick promotion.
Even after being hired, the evaluation continues. Many contracts begin with a probation period of three to six months, during which either side can end the agreement easily. As one HR manager puts it, "The interview shows us who you say you are. Probation shows us who you really are."
